passage:
Bidisha, in Class 11, pinned her whole week to the wall: school, three coaching batches, bus rides, homework. She added it up with a pencil and stared at the total: sixty-two hours, and not one for rest. She was not lazy; the week was simply too full.

She compared her batches. Two of them explained ideas she had not understood at school; the third repeated the school lesson. She dropped the third, and the hours it freed went into working problems alone and sleeping properly.

Irfan kept all his batches because Kamal and the others did. He sat in chairs from morning to nine at night. His notebooks were full, but he could not remember the lectures, and his test marks stayed flat month after month.

Noticing a heavy, grey feeling every afternoon, Bidisha added two lines to her calendar in pen: a thirty-minute walk, and Sunday afternoon free. They were as fixed as her classes. When a friend asked whether that was wasted time, she said, "It's what lets the rest stick."

qa.q: How many hours a week did Bidisha's timetable add up to?
qa.a: It added up to sixty-two hours.

qa.q: How did Bidisha's changes to her batches differ from Irfan's habit, and what happened to their results?
qa.a: Bidisha kept the two batches that explained ideas, freeing time to practise and sleep, while Irfan stayed in every batch and his marks stayed flat.

qa.q: What might Irfan feel when his marks stay flat?
qa.a: Discouraged and worn out, since long days bring no visible progress.

qa.q: What could Irfan try?
qa.a: Irfan could add up his week, find which batches help most, and free some time for practice and rest.

grounding: Four approaches to coaching overload: auditing the timetable, keeping the batches that help most, attending everything from fear, and scheduling rest and exercise.

passage:
Rohan chose one beginner Python course and pinned a note above his desk: one lesson a day. When friends shared links to other courses, he said, "After mine." Only when the last lesson was done did he write his first little script, a cricket quiz.

Uma, Jaya and Indu met every Friday, each with one solved problem to show. The rule was simple: if someone skipped, the other two messaged them. In dull weeks, those Friday meetings kept all three going.

Dev watched video after video and nodded along. He felt he was learning. Then his teacher opened a blank editor and asked him to write a loop that printed one to ten. His fingers stayed above the keys. All this time he had copied what the screen showed and had never typed a line himself.

Three weeks later, looking over his history, Dev saw nothing new since the start. He deleted the video list from his home screen and started with small exercises. He opened a video only when he was stuck, and typed every line himself.

qa.q: What did Rohan write after finishing the course?
qa.a: He wrote his first little script, a cricket quiz.

qa.q: How did the Friday group's routine differ from Dev's video watching, and what were the results?
qa.a: The group brought one solved problem each week and messaged whoever skipped, which kept all three going, while Dev only followed videos and could not write a loop in a blank editor.

qa.q: What was Dev feeling with his fingers above the keys?
qa.a: Embarrassed and stuck, since he had felt he was learning but could not begin.

qa.q: What could Dev do next?
qa.a: Dev could keep solving small exercises first and share his code with a friend at a regular time.

grounding: Four approaches to learning to code online: one course to the end, a study group, hopping between tutorials, and switching method after a review.

passage:
Preeti had been offered a job in Pune; Sachin's work was in Nashik, and each had a lot to say. That night they wrote separate lists. Hers: career growth, then family closeness, then money. His: family closeness, then money, then her happiness. Reading them side by side, they saw that they both put family first.

Next they made a grid for three options: stay put, relocate, or a year on trial. They chose criteria, gave each a weight, and scored each option. The total did not decide anything, but the argument became a conversation.

Nirmala, a friend of Preeti's, had faced the same question with her husband Deepak. He said the same reasons again, louder each time, and ended with, "After all I've done for you." Nirmala said yes to stop the fight. Months later, over a burnt dinner, she snapped about something else entirely, and it took days to settle.

Preeti and Sachin chose the trial year. At six months they sat down: the weekends were too long apart. They did not cancel the plan. They found a flat with a shorter commute and set a visit schedule.

qa.q: Which three options did Preeti and Sachin score?
qa.a: They scored staying put, relocating, or a year on trial.

qa.q: How did Nirmala's outcome differ from Preeti and Sachin's, and why?
qa.a: Nirmala's husband repeated his reasons and used guilt, so she gave in and resentment surfaced in a later fight, while Preeti and Sachin compared lists and scores and adjusted the plan at six months.

qa.q: What was Nirmala feeling when she said yes?
qa.a: Worn down and unheard, wanting only to stop the fight.

qa.q: What could Nirmala do now?
qa.a: Nirmala could tell Deepak calmly what she gave up and ask to go through her priorities and his together.

grounding: Four approaches to a marriage disagreement over a move: separate priority lists, a scored grid, pressure with guilt, and revisiting after a trial.

passage:
Yogesh wanted a remote-control car that cost Rs 600. His weekly pocket money was Rs 50. He did the division on the back of his notebook: twelve weeks. It looked far, but it looked possible, so he kept going.

He asked his mother, Dolma, whether he could earn something extra. She said Rs 10 if he washed the family car every Sunday. Sunday after Sunday the jar filled faster, and the wait became shorter than twelve weeks.

Sarita also got money every week, and every day after school she stopped at the shop for chips and a sheet of stickers. Nobody added it up. After a month she tipped out the jar and found a few coins at the bottom, and no idea where the rest had gone.

Yogesh's patience wore thin in the sixth week. The car still seemed far. He wrote a new number on the jar: 200. When it reached 200, he did a little dance in the hallway. Then he wrote the next target underneath and kept going.

qa.q: How much did the remote-control car cost?
qa.a: It cost Rs 600.

qa.q: Why did Sarita's jar end up almost empty while Yogesh's kept filling?
qa.a: Sarita spent on chips and stickers and nobody added it up, while Yogesh worked out his weeks, earned extra on Sundays and set a smaller number on the jar when he felt discouraged.

qa.q: What was Yogesh feeling in the sixth week?
qa.a: Discouraged and impatient, because the car still seemed far away.

qa.q: What could Sarita do next?
qa.a: Sarita could keep a small tally of what she spends and set a goal with her weekly amount so she can see the finish line.

grounding: Four approaches to saving for a toy: dividing the price by weekly money, earning extra, spending on small things, and setting a smaller first target.

passage:
Aarav wanted to sleep over at his friend's house. He had learned that Papa said yes more easily after dinner, with the news off and his feet up. So Aarav helped clear the plates, waited, and asked then.

Nazia was after a bicycle. Before she spoke, she wrote three things: why she needed it (to reach class faster), how she would stay safe (helmet, main road only), and how she would help pay (her birthday money and a month of dish duty). When her mother, Gargi, frowned and asked, "What about the traffic?" Nazia already had an answer.

Ganga begged for a mobile phone daily, and when the answer was no, cried at the door. Each day the parents grew firmer. By the third week, the word "phone" made them sigh before Ganga had finished.

A month later, Aarav asked to stay out late at a cousin's engagement party, and was told no. He took a breath. "What would I need to show you so you'd say yes next time?" His father thought and said, "Come home on time from smaller outings, and we'll see." Aarav nodded, and wrote it on his hand.

qa.q: When did Aarav ask about the sleepover?
qa.a: He asked after dinner, once Papa was relaxed.

qa.q: How did Ganga's way of asking differ from Nazia's, and what was the result?
qa.a: Ganga asked daily and cried, so the parents grew firmer, while Nazia prepared reasons, a safety plan and a way to pay part, and was ready for her mother's question.

qa.q: What was Ganga feeling at the door?
qa.a: Frustrated and desperate for the phone, which came out as crying.

qa.q: What could Ganga try instead?
qa.a: Ganga could ask once at a calm moment, give reasons, and ask what would change the answer.

grounding: Four approaches to asking parents for something: choosing the moment, preparing reasons, nagging, and asking what would change a no.

passage:
On the carpet, Avni stacked wooden blocks up high. At the sixth block it swayed and fell. She looked, shrugged, and built it again with the pieces in a new order.

Chandrika whispered to herself, "First the big blocks, then the small ones, then the flag on top." She did exactly that, and the tower grew straight, because she always knew what shape she was making.

Santosh patted his tower and said, "Stay up." He put the red block on top, because red was lucky. The tower wobbled anyway. Santosh glared at the red block. "Bad block," he said, and never looked at the narrow bottom.

Avni's tower fell a second time, then a third. She sat back on her heels. "If it wobbles," she said slowly, "make the bottom wider." Next time she laid four blocks side by side first. The tower wobbled once and stayed.

qa.q: At which block did Avni's first tower fall?
qa.a: It fell at the sixth block.

qa.q: How did Santosh's explanation for the wobble differ from Avni's, and what happened to their towers?
qa.a: Santosh blamed the red block and ignored the narrow bottom, while Avni decided to make the bottom wider and her tower stayed up.

qa.q: What was Santosh feeling when he glared at the red block?
qa.a: Annoyed and let down, because he had trusted the lucky block.

qa.q: How could an adult help Santosh?
qa.a: An adult could build a tower with him, point out the narrow bottom, and let him try a wider one.

grounding: Four approaches to building with blocks: trial and error, a step list, magical thinking, and an if-then rule after collapses.
